rv.q: Its delicate, humorous lyricism is another embodiment of Translations ’ big-souled complexity.
A modest yet exquisite revival directed by Doug Hughes, it makes a rigorous case not only for Brian Friel's pre-eminence... but for the vitality of art in deciphering life.
The play's simple and effective revival at the Irish Rep is directed by Doug Hughes and performed by a capable ensemble cast.
Doug Hughes’ direction is so naturalistic, one forgets this is theater.
There’s something elegiac about the current production of Brian Friel’s Translations now playing at the Irish Repertory Theatre.
In his 1980 play Translations , now being lovingly revived at off-Broadway’s Irish Rep, names are of paramount importance: they represent culture, tradition, even identity.
It's a fascinating, if sometimes wearying, examination of a people being colonized through nonviolent means, namely by gradually replacing the native language with a foreign one.

Its messages still ring true on both a personal and a more global level, as it explores how we connect with each other and what we choose to keep and value of myth, legend, history and culture and that which we choose to leave behind.
This revival—playful, serious, provocative—offers fresh insights into Friel’s 1980 masterpiece.
Doug Hughes directs Friels most political work with sense and sensibility.

cn.t: Critics largely praise Irish Rep's revival of Friel's 1980 masterwork, citing its haunting relevance and strong ensemble. A few find it uneven, but the language-and-identity themes resonate powerfully.
